candidate.answerReason: The segment of length 2a forces another point to be its midpoint. The fourth point forms an equilateral triangle with that midpoint and one endpoint, and the Pythagorean theorem gives b²=3a².

methods.label: Force a midpoint, then use an equilateral triangle
methods.explanation:
The length \(2a\) is exactly the sum of two lengths \(a\), suggesting that three of the points may be collinear. Since the points are distinct, \(a>0\).

Name the endpoints of the segment of length \(2a\) as \(P\) and \(Q\). Among the five remaining distances, only the entry \(b\) might differ from \(a\). Thus at least one of the other two points has distance \(a\) from both \(P\) and \(Q\); call it \(M\). We have
\[
PM+MQ=a+a=PQ.
\]
A nondegenerate triangle has the sum of two sides strictly greater than the third. Equality here forces \(M\) onto \(\overline{PQ}\), and \(PM=MQ=a\) makes it the midpoint.

Let \(T\) be the fourth point. It cannot also have \(PT=QT=a\), since that would force it to be the same midpoint \(M\). Therefore the \(b\)-length joins \(T\) to one endpoint. Interchanging \(P\) and \(Q\) if necessary, we may write
\[
PT=b,\qquad QT=MT=a.
\]
Triangle \(MQT\) is equilateral. Let \(H\) be the midpoint of \(MQ\). Its altitude \(TH\) is perpendicular to the line \(PQ\), and
\[
TH^2=a^2-\left(\frac a2\right)^2=\frac{3a^2}{4}.
\]
Also, \(PH=PM+MH=3a/2\). Applying the Pythagorean theorem to \(PHT\) gives
\[
b^2=\left(\frac{3a}{2}\right)^2+\frac{3a^2}{4}=3a^2.
\]
The equilateral triangle can lie on either side of \(PQ\), and both positions give this same result. Since \(a,b>0\), we obtain \(\boxed{b/a=\sqrt3}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

The shortest-segment fact justifies the equality case. Equilateral and isosceles properties justify the auxiliary altitude, with midpoint arithmetic and square roots supporting the calculation.

review.mathematicalCheck: At most one remaining distance can differ from a, forcing a point M with PM=MQ=a and PQ=2a. Equality forces M to be the midpoint. Distinctness then forces the fourth point to form an equilateral triangle with M and one endpoint. The two Pythagorean calculations give b²=3a², uniquely determining b/a=√3.
